issues.legal_issue: A pending revision of a development plan does not extend the time for acquiring land or prevent a designation from lapsing after the owner serves notice and the authority fails to act within the notice period.
material_facts: A final development plan designated the respondents’ lands for specified purposes, and the statutory acquisition period elapsed without acquisition or commencement of acquisition proceedings.
The landowners served notices requiring acquisition, but the authorities did not acquire the lands or commence acquisition steps within the following six months.
A revised development plan came into force around the time the original plan’s ten-year period expired, and the university argued that the revision suspended or extended the acquisition period.
issues.conclusion: The designation lapsed when the authorities failed to acquire the land or commence acquisition steps within six months of the owners’ notices. The revised plan did not extend the acquisition period or revive the lapsed designation.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 20(1) and 20(2) of the Gujarat Town Planning and Urban Development Act, read with Sections 12 and 17, allow acquisition of designated land but provide that the designation is deemed to lapse if the prescribed acquisition period expires, an owner or interested person serves notice, and the authority does not act within six months. Section 21 requires periodic revision of a development plan and applies Sections 9 to 20 to that revision “so far as may be”; those words import the applicable procedure and do not remove the substantive right conferred by Section 20(2). The statutory lapse is a legal fiction that must receive its full effect. The Court relied on Municipal Corporation of Greater Bombay v. Dr. Hakimwadi Tenants’ Association on the lapse provision as a safeguard for landowners; East End Dwelling Co. Ltd. v. Finsbury Borough Council and the cases following it on giving full effect to legal fictions; and The Land Acquisition Officer, City Improvement Trust Board v. H. Narayanaiah on the meaning of qualified language applying provisions “so far as” they are applicable. It distinguished K.L. Gupta, and held Ahmedabad Urban Development Authority and Murari inapplicable to the issue before it.

rule.if: development_plan_lapse_dispute and land_designated_for_public_purpose and initial_acquisition_period_expired_without_acquisition_or_proceedings and owner_served_acquisition_notice and authority_failed_to_act_within_notice_period and revised_plan_pending

predicates.development_plan_lapse_dispute: The proceeding concerns whether a land designation under a development plan has lapsed because acquisition did not occur in time.
predicates.land_designated_for_public_purpose: A development plan designated the land for a specified public purpose.
predicates.initial_acquisition_period_expired_witho: The prescribed initial period ended without the land being acquired or acquisition proceedings being commenced.
predicates.owner_served_acquisition_notice: The owner or another person interested in the land served a notice requiring the authority to acquire it.
predicates.authority_failed_to_act_within_notice_pe: The authority neither acquired the land nor commenced acquisition steps within the period following the notice.
predicates.revised_plan_pending: A revised development plan was pending or in progress when the lapse question arose.
predicates.designation_lapses_despite_revision: The designation is treated as lapsed, and the revision does not extend it or revive it.

issues.definition: When a development-plan designation is challenged after the initial acquisition period, an interested person has served notice, the authority has not acted within the notice period, and a revised plan is pending, the designation lapses despite the revision.

issues.legal_issue: An appellate court does not investigate an assertion that the hearing included submissions omitted from the judgment when the judicial record has not been promptly corrected by the judges who made it.
material_facts: In an appeal, counsel for one university asserted that additional contentions had been raised in the High Court but were not addressed in its judgment.
The asserted omission was not supported by a substantial question of law or an affidavit from counsel or an officer who had attended the High Court hearing.
The appellants had not asked the High Court judges to correct the record while the matter was still fresh.
issues.conclusion: The Court declined to investigate what had transpired in the High Court. If the appellants wished to challenge the recorded account of the hearing, they had to seek correction from the judges who made the record; any other omitted-contention complaint could be pursued by an appropriate review application.
issues.legal_principle: Under State of Maharashtra v. Ramdas Shrinivas Nayak, statements in a judgment about what transpired in court are conclusive and cannot be contradicted by affidavit or other evidence in a later proceeding. A party who says that the hearing was wrongly recorded must call the matter to the attention of the judges who made the record while it is still fresh. The Court also stated that an assertion that other contentions were not considered should be pursued, if appropriate, by an application for review.

predicates.appeal_challenges_hearing_record: A party in an appeal disputes the judgment’s account of what occurred at an earlier court hearing.
predicates.judgment_omits_alleged_submission: The party asserts that a submission made at the hearing was omitted from the judgment.
predicates.no_prompt_record_correction_sought: The party did not promptly ask the judges who made the record to correct it.

issues.definition: When an appeal disputes the hearing record, alleges an omitted submission, and no prompt correction was sought from the judges who made that record, the appellate court declines to investigate the hearing events.
